ruststream-rust-mqtt is the MQTT 5 broker of RustStream, for the embassy and compio runtimes. The crate has two variants. The device variant needs no heap: the board declares the broker's memory as a static, and a delivery borrows its payload from a receive buffer of it. The heap variant (feature alloc, implied by compio) runs over the rust-mqtt client and fits a compio host, or a device that has a heap. Start with the variant you build for: getting started on a device or getting started on a compio host. Testing a device service shows how to run either on the host before it reaches a board.

This section draws where ruststream-rust-mqtt sits between the MQTT broker and the RustStream runtime. The runner and the handles shows how a connection is owned by one task while the handlers, the publishers and the acknowledgements talk to it. What a delivery and a publish cost states what each of them takes from the device.

A PUBLISH is read from the socket into a receive buffer of the broker's memory, exactly as long as its fixed header says. The delivery holds that buffer and borrows its topic and payload from it, so the payload is not copied between the socket and the handler. The headers of the packet are parsed into the delivery, and the buffer goes back to the broker when the handler settles the delivery or drops it. A packet that reaches several subscriptions is copied once into a receive buffer for each subscription beyond the first. A publish is encoded into one of two send buffers, and the runner writes it. The publisher lends the bytes, and Ok means the packet went out into the session. An acknowledgement is a command in a queue of fixed size, and the runner sends the packet. Nothing is allocated, at startup or per message: every buffer is a part of the MqttState the board declares, and its size is (MESSAGES + 2) * PACKET bytes plus a small part for each subscription.

The client, rust-mqtt 0.6, gives each field it receives a heap buffer of its own, so a delivery takes one buffer for each field: the topic, the payload and each string property. The buffers move into the message without a copy, and they are freed when the message is dropped. A publish copies the bytes of the message into a staging slot. The buffers of a slot keep their capacity, so a publish allocates nothing once the slots have held the largest message the service sends. The publisher lends the bytes, and Ok means the packet went out into the session. An acknowledgement is a command in a queue of fixed size. It allocates nothing, and the runner sends the packet. Every queue is fixed at startup: 32 commands, 8 staging slots and 16 deliveries for each subscription. On compio the network adds one copy for each read: io_uring reads into a buffer it owns, and the client reads out of it.

The repository's code-cost benchmarks count what one message costs a service on the core that runs it: instructions under callgrind and allocations under DHAT, release builds with fat LTO, the difference between a run of 500 and a run of 1000 messages against mosquitto. The device variant runs on the host for the measurement, its app and runner driven on one thread. What one message costs Device variant Heap variant on compio ruststream-rumqttc A delivery at QoS 1, acknowledged 6,866 instructions, 0 allocations 10,210 instructions, 2.18 allocations 8,937 instructions, 1.15 allocations A publish (a reply's cost less a delivery's) 4,297 instructions, 0 allocations 12,085 instructions, 0.29 allocations 8,832 instructions, 6.06 allocations The device service reads and answers raw bytes, while the two others decode and encode a JSON body, so its instructions include no codec. just bench-code measures the heap variant and just bench-code-noalloc the device variant.

One task, the runner, owns the connection to the server. The handles of the service (the subscriptions, the publishers and the acknowledgements of the handlers) reach it through storage that exists from the start: on a device the MqttState of the board, on the heap variant queues the broker creates when it is built.

The runner is the only code that touches the socket. It serves one loop: packets from the server, commands from the handles and the keep-alive timer. Each of the three is a step that completes without waiting for the others, so the acknowledgement of a handler never waits behind a read. The runner takes a receive buffer from the pool, reads one packet into it, exactly as long as the fixed header says, and decodes it as a view over those bytes. A PUBLISH goes to the subscription that matches it, and the delivery holds the buffer: its topic and payload are slices of it. The buffer returns to the pool when the handler settles the delivery. When every receive buffer is held, the runner stops reading the connection until a handler settles one. That is the flow control of the device, and the number of buffers is the MESSAGES of the memory. A publish is encoded by the publisher into one of two send buffers and the runner writes it. The buffer returns to the pool when the runner has written the packet, and a publisher waits for a free one when both are in use. The runner assigns the packet identifiers of QoS 1 and 2, holds a publish back while the server's receive maximum is reached, and completes the handshakes of QoS 2. When the connection ends, by a shutdown or by a loss, the runner answers every command that waits, tells every handle the broker is closed, and waits for the next connect. A handle used after that answers an error and never reports a success the connection did not make.

The runner is the only code that touches the client. It serves one loop: packets from the server, commands from the handles and the keep-alive timer. Each of the three is a step that completes without waiting for the others, so the acknowledgement of a handler never waits behind a read. A subscription has a queue of 16 deliveries. When a queue is full, the runner stops reading the connection until the handler takes one. That is the flow control of the crate. A publish copies its bytes into one of 8 staging slots and sends the runner a command. The slot comes back to the pool when the runner has written the packet. The commands wait in a queue of 32, and a sender waits for room when it is full. When the connection ends, by a shutdown or by a loss, the runner answers every command that waits, tells every handle the broker is closed, and waits for the next connect. A handle used after that answers an error and never reports a success the connection did not make. On a device the runner is a task next to the app's. On a compio host the broker starts it on the core that connects the broker.

MqttBroker connects a service to an MQTT 5 server, and the MqttRunner that comes with it owns the connection. On a device, MqttBroker::new takes the MqttState the board declared as a static and a MqttConfig, and returns the broker with its runner. The state is taken for the life of the program, so one state serves one broker. Building the broker performs no I/O, so the whole service fits the synchronous app builder. The runner performs every read and write on the connection, and the handles of the service (subscriptions, publishers, acknowledgements) talk to it. It waits until the app connects the broker, opens the connection over a network, serves it until the app shuts the broker down or the connection is lost, and then waits for the next connect. A device spawns the runner as a task of its own, next to the task of the app. The app starts only while the runner runs, because connecting the broker waits for the runner to open the connection. The broker moves through three types. connect consumes the broker and returns a ConnectedMqttBroker, and shutdown consumes that and returns a ClosedMqttBroker. A publisher the service kept across the shutdown answers MqttError::NotConnected.

The crate has two variants, chosen by its alloc feature, and each fits one kind of build. The device variant is the default and needs no heap. The crate speaks the protocol itself: a PUBLISH is read into a receive buffer of the state, and the delivery borrows its topic and payload from that buffer. Its settings and descriptors hold &'static str, so they are constants of the firmware. A handler reads the payload as bytes it borrows, with #[derive(Deserialized)], and a reply leaves as the bytes it returns, with #[derive(Serialized)]. The heap variant is the alloc feature, which compio turns on. The broker runs over the rust-mqtt client, which keeps every field it receives in a heap buffer of its own, and the settings hold owned strings. MqttBroker::new(config) takes no state, and on a compio host MqttBroker::compio starts the runner on the core that connects the broker, so the host spawns nothing. A device that has a heap takes this variant too, with alloc and embassy. The guide for a compio host shows it. The features, all off by default: embassy adds the network of a device, alloc selects the heap variant, compio adds the network of a compio host and MqttBroker::compio (and alloc), and testing adds the in-process transport a TestApp connects.

A device service: the handler and the app, then the memory, the runner's task and the start function the board's main calls once its network stack is up. MqttConfig holds where the broker connects and as whom: the address, the client id, the keep-alive, the credentials and the session. On a device every text is a &'static str, so the settings hold no buffer of their own and the firmware keeps them in a const. The password is the device's own: the firmware reads it when it boots and adds it to the constant. On the heap variant the texts are owned, and the service takes the password the deployment hands it when it starts. Building a config performs no I/O. The address is read when the broker connects, and a value the broker cannot connect to is reported there as MqttError::Connect. It is host:port or mqtt://host[:port], with the port defaulting to 1883, and an IPv6 literal keeps its brackets. Another scheme, a port that is not a number and an address with no host are refused. The client id is the identity of the session on the server. It starts empty, which asks the server to assign one, and a session that outlives a connection needs an id of its own. The keep-alive is the interval, in whole seconds, after which the runner pings an idle connection; it defaults to 60 seconds and zero turns pings off. credentials sets the user name and the password, and the Debug form of the config shows the user and never the password. persistent_session resumes the session the server keeps for the client id instead of starting a clean one, and asks the server to keep it for the given time after the connection ends. The server then redelivers the QoS 1 and QoS 2 messages that a previous connection left unacknowledged.

The server on the plant network, as the valve valve-1, with a session the server keeps for ten minutes. A device keeps the address, the client id, the keep-alive and the session in a const, and adds the password it was provisioned with when it boots. examples/device/device_config.rs /// The server on the plant network, as this valve. These texts are literals of the firmware, so /// the settings are a constant. The server keeps the session for ten minutes after the /// connection ends and redelivers what the valve had not acknowledged. const VALVE: MqttConfig = MqttConfig::new("mqtt://192.168.1.10:1883") .client_id("valve-1") .keep_alive(Duration::from_secs(30)) .persistent_session(Duration::from_secs(600)); /// The settings with the password the plant provisioned into this valve, which the firmware /// reads when it boots: a secret is not a literal of the firmware. const fn provisioned(password: &'static str) -> MqttConfig { VALVE.credentials("valve-1", password) }

MqttState is the memory a broker of the device variant owns: the receive buffers a delivery borrows from, the send buffers a publish is encoded into, the table of subscriptions and the channels between the handles and the runner. It is one value of known size that the board declares as a static, so nothing is allocated, at startup or per message. Three numbers fix its size, and they are the type's parameters: MqttState<MESSAGES, PACKET, SUBSCRIPTIONS> with the defaults 4, 1024 and 8. The broker, its runner and its deliveries carry the same three numbers, and a broker over the defaults is named MqttBroker alone. MESSAGES is the number of receive buffers. A delivery holds one from its arrival until its handler settles it or drops it, so this is how many deliveries wait or are in hand at once. The session asks the server to keep at most one fewer QoS 1 and 2 deliveries in flight, so a buffer stays free for the server's answers. When every buffer is held, the runner stops reading the connection until a handler settles one: that is the back-pressure of the device, and it reaches the server through the TCP window. A device whose handlers are slow, or that acknowledge late, takes more buffers; the minimum is two. PACKET is the size in bytes of each receive buffer and each send buffer, so it is the largest packet in either direction. The session announces it to the server as its maximum packet size, and the server never sends a larger one. A publish that does not fit is refused before it is sent, and the message is handed back to the caller. The packet holds the fixed header, the topic and the properties besides the payload, so the largest payload is smaller than PACKET. The minimum is 64. SUBSCRIPTIONS is how many subscriptions are open at once, one for each mounted descriptor. The minimum is one. A PUBLISH that reaches several subscriptions is copied into a receive buffer for each one beyond the first, so it holds as many buffers as there are subscriptions it matches. The memory it takes is about (MESSAGES + 2) * PACKET bytes, the two being the send buffers, plus a small part for each subscription and each message. The numbers are checked when the state is built, in a const context, so a value below a minimum does not compile.

Six deliveries of up to 512 bytes and four subscriptions, about 4 KiB of the board's RAM. More frames than buffers pass through it, because a settled buffer returns to the broker. examples/device/device_memory.rs /// Six deliveries of up to 512 bytes, and four subscriptions: about 4 KiB of the board's RAM. type Memory = MqttState<6, 512, 4>; static MQTT: ConstStaticCell<Memory> = ConstStaticCell::new(MqttState::new()); /// The broker over that memory, named by the same three numbers. type Mqtt = MqttBroker<6, 512, 4>;

Network is the link the runner connects over: it opens a stream to a host and a port, and it sleeps on the clock of the runtime the runner runs on. The stream is anything that reads and writes through embedded-io-async, and a read of it must be cancel-safe: the runner stops waiting for the next packet of the server when a handle sends it work, and picks the read up again afterwards. A device uses EmbassyNetwork (feature embassy): a TCP socket on an embassy-net stack, over a receive buffer and a send buffer that the task of the runner owns. The runner reads a packet from the socket straight into a receive buffer of the broker's memory, exactly as long as the fixed header of the packet says, so a PUBLISH stays where it arrived and the delivery borrows from it. A host name in the address is resolved by the DNS client of the stack, and an IPv4 literal is used as it is. A failure is an EmbassyConnectError: the name did not resolve, or the TCP connection failed. A compio host, on the heap variant, uses CompioNetwork (feature compio), and MqttBroker::compio starts the runner over it. io_uring reads into a buffer it owns until the read completes, so a task of the connection reads the stream into owned buffers and the client reads out of them. That costs one copy per read, and a read the client stops waiting for loses nothing. A board with another link, such as a TLS session or the socket of a modem, implements Network for that link; the rustdoc of the trait shows a board's network. Whatever the network, the runner takes it as an argument of MqttRunner::run.

MqttPublish is the publish policy of a mount: the quality of service and the retain flag of every message it publishes. A policy is a plain declaration that holds no connection, and the runtime pairs it with the connected broker into an MqttPublisher. qos defaults to Qos::AtLeastOnce and retain to false. The policy is also the default of the broker, so a reply and a retry copy leave through it unless the mount names another. On a device the publisher encodes the message straight into a send buffer of the broker's memory, which the runner writes, and a message that does not fit the packet is refused with the message handed back. On the heap variant the publisher copies the bytes of a message into a staging slot of the broker, whose buffers keep their capacity, so a publish allocates nothing once the slots have held the largest message the service sends. Ok means the PUBLISH packet went out into the session; at QoS 1 and 2 the session keeps the message until the server acknowledges it. A publish to a topic no server takes, such as one with a wildcard, is refused with MqttError::Publish, and a publish after the shutdown answers MqttError::NotConnected. A refused publish hands its message back.

A device reports every reading in degrees, and the reports are sent exactly once. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_publishing_policy.rs /// Reports every reading in degrees: the return value is the reply. #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("sensors/temp"), reply)] async fn report(reading: &Reading) -> Report { Report { celsius: i16::try_from((i32::from(reading.millivolts) - 500) / 10).unwrap_or(i16::MAX), } } #[ruststream::app(runtime = embassy)] fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| { // Reports are sent exactly once. b.include(report) .out_reply(MqttPublish::default().qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce)) }) } examples/manual/mqtt_publishing_policy.rs /// Reports every reading in degrees: the return value is the reply. struct Reporter; impl Handle<Reading, Report> for Reporter { fn handle( &self, reading: &Reading, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Report, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Report { celsius: i16::try_from((i32::from(reading.millivolts) - 500) / 10).unwrap_or(i16::MAX), })) } } fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| { // Reports are sent exactly once. b.include( subscriber("sensors/temp", Reporter) .map_source(|_| MqttTopic::new("sensors/temp")) .reply() .to("reports/temp") .build(), ) .out_reply(MqttPublish::default().qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce)) }) }

Headers travel as MQTT 5 user properties, and content-type, reply-to and correlation-id take the matching properties of the protocol. A serde struct is the contract of a message's headers, and each field is one property whose value is a string. The handler reads them with the Headers extractor, and a publish writes them with with_headers. A textual content type also sets the payload format indicator, and correlation-id is binary on the wire. A header whose name or value is not UTF-8 text without control characters is refused with MqttError::Publish, except the correlation id. The header partition-key (PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) is the key that keyed workers order a subscription's deliveries by.

The state leaves with the trace id the command arrived with. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_publishing_headers.rs /// The state goes out with the trace the command arrived with. #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("valves/v1/set"))] async fn set( command: &Command, Headers(trace): Headers<Trace>, Out(states): Out<impl Publisher<Options = MqttPublishOptions>, States>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let state = State { open: command.open }; if states .message(&state) .with_headers(&trace) .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app(runtime = embassy)] fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(set).out(States, MqttPublish::default()) }) } examples/manual/mqtt_publishing_headers.rs /// The state goes out with the trace the command arrived with. struct Set; impl<Entry> Handle<Command, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Set where Entry: OutEntry<States, Wire: Publisher<Options = MqttPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, command: &Command, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Headers(trace) = Headers::<Trace>::from_context(ctx).await?; let state = State { open: command.open }; outs.get(States) .message(&state) .with_headers(&trace) .publish() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("valves/v1/set", Set) .map_source(|_| MqttTopic::new("valves/v1/set")) .build(), ) .out(States, MqttPublish::default()) }) }

A retained message is kept by the server, which hands the last one of each topic to every new subscription that is not shared. retain(true) on the policy retains every message of the mount, and the step retains one. A dashboard that starts later reads the state without waiting for the next change. Publishing an empty retained payload clears the topic. The subscription receives the retained message at the lower of the two levels, as any other delivery.

The state of the valve is retained, so a subscriber that joins later reads the latest one. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_publishing_retained.rs /// The valve's state is retained, so a subscriber that joins later reads the latest one. #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("valves/v1/position"))] async fn track( position: &Position, Out(states): Out<impl Publisher<Options = MqttPublishOptions>, States>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let state = State { open: position.percent > 0, }; if states.message(&state).retain(true).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app(runtime = embassy)] fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(track).out(States, MqttPublish::default()) }) } examples/manual/mqtt_publishing_retained.rs /// The valve's state is retained, so a subscriber that joins later reads the latest one. struct Track; impl<Entry> Handle<Position, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Track where Entry: OutEntry<States, Wire: Publisher<Options = MqttPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, position: &Position, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let state = State { open: position.percent > 0, }; outs.get(States) .message(&state) .retain(true) .publish() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("valves/v1/position", Track) .map_source(|_| MqttTopic::new("valves/v1/position")) .build(), ) .out(States, MqttPublish::default()) }) }

The steps qos and retain on the publish builder reopen, for one message, what the policy of the mount fixed. MqttPublishSteps is in the prelude, and the steps appear on a builder over an MQTT publisher and on no other broker's. A setting that a call leaves unset keeps the value of the policy. A handler body that takes a step bounds its slot with Out<impl Publisher<Options = MqttPublishOptions>, Slot>, and that is the one place a body names a type of this crate. The settings of one call travel as an MqttPublishOptions, and a test reads them back with with_options.

A state change is sent exactly once and retained. An ack sends PUBACK at QoS 1 and PUBREC at QoS 2; QoS 0 has no acknowledgement. A message settles when the handler returns, and the quality of service of the delivery decides what that sends. At QoS 1 and 2 the server keeps a delivery until it is acknowledged, and the client finishes the QoS 2 handshake on its own once the server releases the message. A QoS 0 delivery has no acknowledgement packet, so settling it answers AckError::Unsupported, which the runtime logs as a warning. drop acknowledges the delivery too, because an acknowledgement is the only final answer MQTT has, and the server never sends the message again. retry asks for a negative acknowledgement, which MQTT does not have, and retry_after is the outcome that tries again later. The acknowledgement goes to the runner, which sends it; a delivery settled after the broker shut down answers AckError::Broker, carrying MqttError::NotConnected.

A device agent applies the commands it knows and drops the rest; both answers settle the delivery. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_settlement_ack.rs /// The subscription reads at `QoS` 1, so returning from the handler acknowledges the delivery with /// a PUBACK. A command the device does not know is dropped: on MQTT that acknowledges it as well, /// and the server never sends it again. #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("devices/dev42/commands").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce))] async fn apply(command: &Command) -> HandlerOutcome { match command.action.as_str() { "reboot" | "reset" => HandlerOutcome::ack(), _ => HandlerOutcome::drop(), } } #[ruststream::app(runtime = embassy)] fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(apply)) } examples/manual/mqtt_settlement_ack.rs /// The subscription reads at `QoS` 1, so returning from the handler acknowledges the delivery with /// a PUBACK. A command the device does not know is dropped: on MQTT that acknowledges it as well, /// and the server never sends it again. struct Apply; impl Handle<Command> for Apply { fn handle( &self, command: &Command, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { ready(match command.action.as_str() { "reboot" | "reset" => Ok(()), _ => Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()), }) } } fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| { let commands = MqttTopic::new("devices/dev42/commands").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce); b.include( subscriber("devices/dev42/commands", Apply) .map_source(|_| commands) .build(), ) }) }

The subscription reads telemetry at QoS 0. The handler settles each delivery as usual, and nothing is sent to the server. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_settlement_qos0.rs /// Telemetry at `QoS` 0: the next reading replaces a lost one, so the subscription asks for no /// acknowledgement. The outcome still settles the delivery in the service; the runtime has no /// packet to send for it and logs that it is unsupported. #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("sensors/temp").qos(Qos::AtMostOnce))] async fn store(reading: &Reading) -> HandlerOutcome { if reading.celsius < -40 { return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app(runtime = embassy)] fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(store)) } examples/manual/mqtt_settlement_qos0.rs /// Telemetry at `QoS` 0: the next reading replaces a lost one, so the subscription asks for no /// acknowledgement. The outcome still settles the delivery in the service; the runtime has no /// packet to send for it and logs that it is unsupported. struct Store; impl Handle<Reading> for Store { fn handle( &self, reading: &Reading, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { ready(if reading.celsius < -40 { Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } else { Ok(()) }) } } fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| { let temp = MqttTopic::new("sensors/temp").qos(Qos::AtMostOnce); b.include( subscriber("sensors/temp", Store) .map_source(|_| temp) .build(), ) }) }

MQTT has no negative acknowledgement, so retry answers AckError::Unsupported and leaves the delivery unacknowledged. A nack with requeue set is what retry asks for. The transport has no packet for it, so the delivery stays unacknowledged on the server, which redelivers it when a persistent session resumes. The runtime logs the unsupported answer as a warning and does not send the message again by itself. A handler that wants the delivery back within the session answers retry_after. A nack without requeue is a drop, and it acknowledges.

A job that is not ready to run is answered with retry, and the runtime sees one call. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_settlement_nack.rs /// A job id of zero is not ready to run. `retry` asks for a negative acknowledgement, which MQTT /// does not have: the delivery stays unacknowledged, and the server sends it again when a /// persistent session resumes. #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("jobs/run"))] async fn run(job: &Job) -> HandlerOutcome { if job.id == 0 { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app(runtime = embassy)] fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(run)) } examples/manual/mqtt_settlement_nack.rs /// A job id of zero is not ready to run. `retry` asks for a negative acknowledgement, which MQTT /// does not have: the delivery stays unacknowledged, and the server sends it again when a /// persistent session resumes. struct Run; impl Handle<Job> for Run { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { ready(if job.id == 0 { Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()) } else { Ok(()) }) } } fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("jobs/run", Run) .map_source(|_| MqttTopic::new("jobs/run")) .build(), ) }) }

retry_after publishes a copy of the delivery after a delay: to its own topic for MqttTopic, to a topic the mount site names for MqttFilter. The server moves nothing on a negative answer, so the copy is a publish made by the service. A subscription on a topic is reached again by publishing to that topic, and the descriptor reports it, so the mount site names nothing. A subscription on a filter reads many topics and reports no address. There the mount names the destination with .out_retry(policy).to(name), and a chain that names none does not compile. The copy comes back to the subscription when the named topic matches the filter. The copy leaves through the policy of out_retry, such as MqttPublish, and carries the retry count in the RETRY_COUNT_HEADER header. On a device the copy waits in the store of the mount, and .retry_capacity::<N>() after the mount sets how many wait at once.

A topic subscription, asked for again in five seconds. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_settlement_retry_after.rs /// The valve is still moving: the job is asked for again in five seconds. A copy that carries its /// retry count is the second attempt, and it is acknowledged. #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("jobs/run"))] async fn run(job: &Job, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let _ = job.id; match ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER) { Some(_) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), None => HandlerOutcome::retry_after(Duration::from_secs(5)), } } #[ruststream::app(runtime = embassy)] fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { // Room for two copies waiting at once. EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(run).retry_capacity::<2>()) } examples/manual/mqtt_settlement_retry_after.rs /// The valve is still moving: the job is asked for again in five seconds. A copy that carries its /// retry count is the second attempt, and it is acknowledged. struct Run; impl Handle<Job> for Run { fn handle( &self, _job: &Job, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { ready(match ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER) { Some(_) => Ok(()), None => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(Duration::from_secs(5))), }) } } fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { // Room for two copies waiting at once. EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("jobs/run", Run) .map_source(|_| MqttTopic::new("jobs/run")) .build(), ) .retry_capacity::<2>() }) }

The mount names jobs/retry, which the filter jobs/+ matches. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_settlement_retry_after.rs /// A filter reads many topics and addresses none of them, so the mount site names where a copy /// goes: `jobs/retry` matches the filter, and the copy comes back to the handler. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("jobs/+"))] async fn reconcile(job: &Job, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let _ = job.id; match ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER) { Some(_) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), None => HandlerOutcome::retry_after(Duration::from_secs(5)), } } #[ruststream::app(runtime = embassy)] fn filter_app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(reconcile) .out_retry(MqttPublish::default()) .to("jobs/retry") .retry_capacity::<2>() }) } examples/manual/mqtt_settlement_retry_after.rs /// A filter reads many topics and addresses none of them, so the mount site names where a copy /// goes: `jobs/retry` matches the filter, and the copy comes back to the handler. struct Reconcile; impl Handle<Job> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, _job: &Job, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { ready(match ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER) { Some(_) => Ok(()), None => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(Duration::from_secs(5))), }) } } fn filter_app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("jobs/+", Reconcile) .map_source(|_| MqttFilter::new("jobs/+")) .build(), ) .out_retry(MqttPublish::default()) .to("jobs/retry") .retry_capacity::<2>() }) }

MqttTopic subscribes to one topic a publisher can name, and answers for its own retry copies. A topic carries no wildcard, so it is a name a publisher can use. A subscription on a topic is reached again by publishing to that topic, which is why the descriptor can say where the copy of a retried delivery goes. A value with a + or a # is refused when the app starts, and the message names MqttFilter as the descriptor that takes it. The topic must not be empty and must be text an MQTT string carries: no control character and no Unicode non-character. qos sets the quality of service the subscription asks for, and shared makes it a shared subscription. A definition written #[subscriber(MqttTopic)] takes its topic from the name given at the mount site.

A valve listens on its own topic. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_subscriptions_topic.rs /// The valve listens on its own topic. #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("valves/v1/set"))] async fn set(command: &Command) -> HandlerOutcome { let _ = command.open; HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app(runtime = embassy)] fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(set)) } examples/manual/mqtt_subscriptions_topic.rs /// The valve listens on its own topic. struct Set; impl Handle<Command> for Set { fn handle( &self, _command: &Command, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(())) } } fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("valves/v1/set", Set) .map_source(|_| MqttTopic::new("valves/v1/set")) .build(), ) }) }

Two handlers on one filter are one subscription on the server, so they take the messages in turn. A server holds one subscription per filter, and subscribing the same filter again replaces it. So the subscriptions an app opens on one filter are members of one route: they share its deliveries, and each message reaches one of them, the next in order. The members of a share group work the same way. A handler that must see every message reads a filter of its own.

Two handlers on jobs/+: the first takes the first message, the second takes the next, and so on. MqttFilter subscribes to every topic its wildcards match: + matches one level and # matches the rest. One filter reads many topics, so it addresses none of them. A retry copy cannot go to a filter, and the mount site names where it goes. The delivery keeps the topic it was published to, and MqttMessage::topic returns it. A filter that is not a valid topic filter is refused when the app starts. qos and shared work as on MqttTopic. A definition written #[subscriber(MqttFilter)] takes its filter from the name given at the mount site.

Every sensor of the first floor reports on a topic of its own. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_subscriptions_filter.rs /// Every sensor of the first floor reports on a topic of its own. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("floor-1/+/temp"))] async fn log(reading: &Reading) -> HandlerOutcome { let _ = reading.celsius; HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app(runtime = embassy)] fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(log)) } examples/manual/mqtt_subscriptions_filter.rs /// Every sensor of the first floor reports on a topic of its own. struct Log; impl Handle<Reading> for Log { fn handle( &self, _reading: &Reading, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(())) } } fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("floor-1/+/temp", Log) .map_source(|_| MqttFilter::new("floor-1/+/temp")) .build(), ) }) }

Qos picks at most once, at least once or exactly once; a delivery arrives at the lower of the publisher's and the subscription's level. A subscription names its level with qos(..) on MqttTopic or MqttFilter, and the default is Qos::AtLeastOnce. Level QoS What the protocol does AtMostOnce 0 sends the message once, with no acknowledgement; a message lost on the way is gone AtLeastOnce 1 resends until the receiver answers PUBACK; a message may arrive twice ExactlyOnce 2 a four-packet handshake, so the message arrives once The server sends each message at the lower of two levels: the one its publisher sent it at and the one the subscription asked for. So a QoS 2 subscription receives a QoS 0 publish at QoS 0, and MqttMessage::qos tells the level a delivery arrived at. A delivery at QoS 1 or 2 is acknowledged when the handler settles it. The level a publish is sent at is a setting of the publish policy.

Telemetry read at most once, because the next reading replaces a lost one, and a valve command read exactly once. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_subscriptions_qos.rs /// Telemetry is read at most once: the next reading replaces a lost one. #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("sensors/temp").qos(Qos::AtMostOnce))] async fn store(reading: &Reading) -> HandlerOutcome { let _ = reading.celsius; HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// A valve command is applied exactly once. #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("valves/v1/set").qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce))] async fn set(command: &Command) -> HandlerOutcome { let _ = command.open; HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app(runtime = embassy)] fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(store).include(set)) } examples/manual/mqtt_subscriptions_qos.rs /// Telemetry is read at most once: the next reading replaces a lost one. struct Store; impl Handle<Reading> for Store { fn handle( &self, _reading: &Reading, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(())) } } /// A valve command is applied exactly once. struct Set; impl Handle<Command> for Set { fn handle( &self, _command: &Command, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(())) } } fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| { let temp = MqttTopic::new("sensors/temp").qos(Qos::AtMostOnce); let valve = MqttTopic::new("valves/v1/set").qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce); b.include( subscriber("sensors/temp", Store) .map_source(|_| temp) .build(), ) .include( subscriber("valves/v1/set", Set) .map_source(|_| valve) .build(), ) }) }

A shared subscription hands each message to one member of a group, so boards that run the same service share the work. shared(group) on MqttTopic or MqttFilter subscribes through $share/<group>/<filter>, an MQTT 5 feature. The server gives each matching message to one subscription of the group instead of to every one. The group name must not be empty and must not contain /, + or #; the descriptor refuses it when the app starts. The server sends no retained message to a shared subscription when it joins. A retry copy of a delivery goes to the plain topic: the $share prefix is a name for subscribing, and a publish to it would reach a topic of that literal spelling.

Every board runs this service, and the server gives each job to one of them. The embedded TestApp runs a device service on the host with the broker connected in process, and the test drives it with publish, advance and assertions. The test hands the production app its broker, built over a static memory the test declares as the board does, and addresses the broker by its type: tb.broker::<MqttBroker>(). The runner is not needed, because the in-process transport replaces the connection. It is a model of the server: it keeps the subscriptions, the retained message of each topic and the share groups, matches filters with wildcards, and delivers at the lower of the two levels. message(..).publish() is a publish of another client of the server, at QoS 1 and not retained. The clock is the test's: advance moves it, and a retry_after copy comes back once its delay has passed. The deliveries a test holds at once are bounded by the memory of the broker: a handler that has not settled a delivery keeps its receive buffer, as on the device. A persistent session and its redelivery, the receive window and the handshakes behind QoS 1 and 2 belong to the server, and the live stand tests them. The assertions on the options of a publish, such as with_options, read the steps and the retain flag of an Out slot.

A job is answered, and the answer is read from the topic it was published to. A live test runs the service against a real server, for what the in-process transport leaves to the server: the connection, a persistent session and its redelivery, the handshakes behind QoS 1 and 2. The stand is a mosquitto container with an anonymous listener and one that needs a password. just test-brokers starts it, runs the live suites with RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE set, and stops it. A live test reads the address of the stand from MQTT_TEST_URL; the variable RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE turns a missing stand into a failure, so a test that skipped itself is noticed. The test below runs the service on compio and talks to it as a second client of the same server.

A job published to the server is answered by the service, and the answer comes back through a subscription of the test. examples/mqtt_testing_live.rs #[test] fn a_job_is_answered_through_the_server() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { // The stand is `just test-brokers`; a run without one has nothing to test. let Ok(url) = std::env::var("MQTT_TEST_URL") else { return Ok(()); }; Runtime::new()?.block_on(async { let running = app().start().await?; // The test is another client of the same server. let client = MqttBroker::compio(MqttConfig::new(url).client_id("tester")) .connect() .await?; let mut answers = MqttTopic::new("live/done").subscribe(&client).await?; let jobs = MqttPublish::default().pair(&client).await?; jobs.publish(OutgoingMessage::new("live/jobs", br#"{"id":7}"#), None) .await .map_err(PublishMessageError::into_error)?; let mut deliveries = core::pin::pin!(answers.stream()); let answer = deliveries.next().await.ok_or("the subscription ended")??; assert_eq!(answer.payload(), br#"{"id":7}"#); answer.ack().await?; client.shutdown().await?; running.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) }) }
On a compio host the service is the handler and the app. MqttBroker::compio starts the runner on the core that connects the broker, over the TCP stream of compio, so nothing is spawned by hand.

documents.t: A host has a heap, and the crate's heap variant uses it: the alloc feature, which compio turns on. The broker runs over the rust-mqtt client, the settings hold owned strings, and handlers decode their payload with the codec of the framework, json among them. The broker needs no MqttState, because the client allocates what it receives. A device that has a heap takes the same variant with alloc and embassy. It builds the broker with MqttBroker::new(config) and spawns the runner as a task, as in getting started on a device, and the handlers use serde types. A device without a heap takes the device variant.

A device service has no heap. The broker's memory is a static the board declares, a delivery borrows its payload from a receive buffer of that memory, and a reply is encoded into a send buffer of it. This guide builds a valve board that applies the commands published to valves/v1/set and reports the state it reached. A service has three parts: the handler and the app, the task of the runner that owns the MQTT connection, and the main of the board that spawns both.

cargo add ruststream --no-default-features --features embassy,macros cargo add ruststream-rust-mqtt --features embassy cargo add embassy-executor embassy-net static_cell The embassy feature of the broker crate adds EmbassyNetwork, the runner's network over an embassy-net stack. The broker crate is the device variant until its alloc feature is on, and the framework follows: a feature of ruststream that needs a heap, such as json, turns the framework's alloc on, and the broker crate then asks for its own alloc feature as well. A device that has a heap takes the heap variant the same way.

The handler takes a Command and returns the State it reaches. Command is the payload as the bytes that arrived: it borrows them from the receive buffer of the broker, so reading a command copies nothing. State is the bytes that leave, and the reply is encoded straight into a send buffer. #[ruststream::app(runtime = embassy)] turns the app function into an embassy task, app::task. Macros Manual examples/device/device_service.rs /// A command as the controller sends its bytes, borrowed from the broker's receive buffer. #[derive(Deserialized)] struct Command<'a>(&'a [u8]); /// The state the valve reports, as the bytes that leave. #[derive(Outgoing, Serialized)] #[outgoing(name = "valves/v1/state")] struct State(&'static [u8]); /// Moves the valve and reports where it is. #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("valves/v1/set"), reply)] async fn set(command: &Command<'_>) -> State { match command.0 { b"open" => State(b"opened"), _ => State(b"closed"), } } #[ruststream::app(runtime = embassy)] fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(set).out_reply(MqttPublish::default())) } examples/manual/device_service.rs /// A command as the controller sends its bytes, borrowed from the broker's receive buffer. struct Command<'a>(&'a [u8]); // `#[derive(Deserialized)]` by hand: the view borrows the payload, and `&Command<'_>` takes the // lane that reads no codec. impl Deserialized for Command<'_> { type Output<'a> = Command<'a>; type Error = Infallible; fn from_payload(payload: &[u8]) -> Result<Command<'_>, Self::Error> { Ok(Command(payload)) } } impl Input for Command<'_> { type Axis = SoloDeserialized<Command<'static>>; } /// The state the valve reports, as the bytes that leave. struct State(&'static [u8]); // `#[derive(Serialized)]` by hand: the bytes, the wire of a typed publish, the shape of a reply. impl Serialized for State { type Error = Infallible; fn wire_bytes(&self, _buf: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<WireBytes<'_>, Infallible> { Ok(WireBytes::Own(self.0)) } } impl MessageWire for State { type Wire = SerializedWire; } impl ReplyShape for State { type Body = Self; type Headers = (); type Wire = SerializedReply; } // `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with no `name`, by hand: the mount names the destination. impl OutgoingDestination for State { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for State { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// Moves the valve and reports where it is. struct Set; impl<'p> Handle<Command<'p>, State> for Set { fn handle( &self, command: &Command<'p>, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<State, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(match command.0 { b"open" => State(b"opened"), _ => State(b"closed"), })) } } fn app(broker: MqttBroker) -> EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts> { EmbeddedApp::new().with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("valves/v1/set", Set) .map_source(|_| MqttTopic::new("valves/v1/set")) .reply() .to("valves/v1/state") .build(), ) .out_reply(MqttPublish::default()) }) }

MqttState is all the memory the broker owns: the receive buffers deliveries borrow from, the send buffers, and the table of subscriptions. The board declares it as a static and hands it to MqttBroker::new once, which returns the broker with its runner. The runner owns the connection: it opens it when the app connects the broker, and every read, write and acknowledgement goes through it. So the board spawns two tasks, the runner's over the network stack and the app's with the broker. The socket buffers live in the runner's task, and their size is the board's choice.
